newsitem.title: JORDAN: Turkey's Ciller calls for Mideast security group.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller calls for Mideast security group.

text.p: Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller called on Tuesday for a Middle East security organisation to help reduce regional conflict.
"We feel that a security system in the region is a must," Ciller told a news conference in Jordan after talks with Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.

Ciller, who said the two countries had agreed on cooperation in defence and combatting "terrorism", was due to discuss the security organisation later on Tuesday with Crown Prince Hassan, who has campaigned in the past for such a mechanism.
"We very much support the regional security system as put forward by the crown prince. This was also put forward by Turkey in the late 1980s," Ciller said.
She gave no details of the proposed organisation, but said it could be a Middle East counterpart to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

Turkish diplomats said it could involve "conflict prevention centres" as well as embracing wider elements of multi-lateral Middle East peace talks, including cooperation on water resources, refugees, and economic aid.
"All of these constitute in the long run parts of Middle East security," Turkey's ambassador to Jordan Suha Omar told reporters.
Plans for a regional security or conflict prevention body in the area have been floated before, most recently by British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind earlier this month.
Rifkind said membership should be open to all states including Iraq and Iran. Tehran said the idea was colonialist and regional heavyweight Egypt dismissed it as premature.

Ciller said her talks with Jordanian officials also aimed to boost weak economic ties, including improving trade, cooperating in privatisation plans, linking electricity networks and following up a Jordanian request to buy water from Turkey.
"Along the lines of defence (and) anti-terrorism programmes...we did take various steps... We decided to act against terrorism together," Ciller said, without elaborating.
Turkey's security forces have fought a 12-year battle against Kurdish rebels seeking self-rule in southeastern areas near the border with Iraq.
Jordan was one of the few Arab countries not to criticise publicly a proposed Turkish security zone in north Iraq against the rebels forces.
Ciller said Jordan and Turkey, suffering economically from six years of sanctions imposed on neighbouring Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, "shared the same strategy" towards Baghdad.
Kabariti, whose government turned against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and called for change in Baghdad, said on Monday he and Ciller discussed efforts to get the sanctions lifted.
Ciller said they also agreed to form a defence committee to discuss cooperation.
Diplomats said Turkey was offering to maintain Jordanian fighter jets and to provide training and spare parts, as well as looking into possible joint venture defence projects.
